# Gradient Computation and Back-Propagation

Also called: Differentiable Volume Rendering Gradients, Back-Propagation in Gaussian Splatting

## Overview
Gradient Computation and Back-Propagation provides the mathematical and algorithmic foundation for optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting parameters by computing the derivative of a loss function with respect to scene primitives (means, covariances, opacities, colors). It solves the problem of enabling end-to-end training of radiance fields by establishing a differentiable path from the rendered image pixels to the 3D parameters. It sets itself apart from standard rendering by explicitly deriving chain-rule gradients through the alpha-compositing equation and coordinate transformations, allowing for GPU-accelerated, tile-based accumulation of gradients into packed buffers [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism relies on the differentiable alpha-compositing equation and the chain rule. The rendered color $I(x,y)$ at pixel $(x,y)$ is computed as:
$$ I(x,y) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} T_k(x,y) \alpha_k(x,y) \sigma(\mathbf{c}_k) $$
where $T_k(x,y) = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} (1 - \alpha_j(x,y))$ is the transmittance, $\alpha_k$ is the opacity, and $\sigma(\mathbf{c}_k)$ is the color contribution of the $k$-th Gaussian [S1, unofficial].

Gradients are accumulated per-pixel directly into packed `half2` buffers via `half2` atomicAdd over two-channel gradient groups, followed by a lightweight post-pass that unpacks to legacy FP16 arrays. This design omits block-local reductions to align with accuracy-throughput goals [S1, unofficial].

For geometric parameters (position $\mathbf{x}_i$, scale $s_i$, rotation $\theta_i$), gradients are computed via the chain rule through the coordinate transformation from 3D space to 2D image space. The gradient of the image intensity $I(x,y)$ with respect to a primitive's position $\mathbf{x}_i$ is:
$$ \frac{\partial I(x,y)}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i} = \frac{\partial I(x,y)}{\partial M_i(x,y)} \left( \frac{\partial M_i(x,y)}{\partial u} \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i} + \frac{\partial M_i(x,y)}{\partial v} \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i} \right) $$
where $M_i$ is the primitive mask, and $u,v$ are local coordinates derived from the projection [S1, unofficial]. The terms $\frac{\partial M_i}{\partial u}$ and $\frac{\partial M_i}{\partial v}$ are calculated exactly using the rendering equations, while $\frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i}$ and $\frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i}$ are derived from the projection Jacobian [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [ToF Gradient Computation for Gaussian Splatting](9733-tof-gradient-computation-for-gaussian-splatting.md)
Computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the opacity parameter $\alpha_k$ specifically for Time-of-Flight (ToF) image formation models, such as those involving phasor or quad pixel signals [9733-tof-gradient-computation-for-gaussian-splatting]. It extends standard 3DGS back-propagation by introducing squared transmittance terms in the recursive accumulation, addressing the non-linear interaction between opacity and ToF signal intensity [9733-tof-gradient-computation-for-gaussian-splatting]. Unlike standard color rendering which uses a linear accumulation of subsequent contributions, ToF signal gradients require a quadratic weighting of the transmittance due to the nature of the signal formation equation [9733-tof-gradient-computation-for-gaussian-splatting]. Choose this when training on ToF data. See [ToF Gradient Computation for Gaussian Splatting](9733-tof-gradient-computation-for-gaussian-splatting.md).

### [Gradient-Weighted Feature Back-Projection](9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection.md)
A training-free method for rendering feature fields in 3D Gaussian Splatting by aggregating 2D feature embeddings from training views into pre-trained 3D Gaussians [9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection]. It solves the problem of assigning semantic or appearance features to 3D Gaussians without the computational cost and memory overhead of training a separate feature field [9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection]. Unlike training-based alternatives like Feature 3DGS, which require 20–30 minutes for optimization, this method completes the aggregation in a single pass through training views, offering a 10x speedup and high-quality 3D segmentation results [9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection]. It sets itself apart by using the rendering gradient (opacity-weighted transmittance) as the back-projection weight, effectively treating the gradient as a measure of Gaussian influence on the final pixel [9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection]. Choose this for semantic segmentation or feature field extraction without retraining. See [Gradient-Weighted Feature Back-Projection](9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection.md).

### [SNS Backward Pass with Intermediate Variable Q](10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q.md)
Computes the gradients of the loss with respect to the 3D Gaussian parameters (mean, skew, rotation, scale, color, opacity) for Skew-Normal Splatting [10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q]. It solves the problem of high computational complexity and intricate coupling between rotation $R$ and scale $S$ in standard 3DGS gradient computation by introducing an intermediate variable $Q = ARS$ [10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q]. Unlike standard 3DGS, which computes gradients w.r.t. 2D image-space variables first, SNS directly evaluates shared auxiliary algebraic terms during the rendering stage to enable efficient closed-form gradient evaluation for 3D parameters in the preprocessing stage [10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q]. Choose this when using Skew-Normal Splatting representations. See [SNS Backward Pass with Intermediate Variable Q](10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q.md).

### [Specular-Aware Gradient Gating](13432-specular-aware-gradient-gating.md)
A training optimization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that suppresses specular reflection artifacts in semi-transparent scenes while preserving the geometric details of transmitted light [13432-specular-aware-gradient-gating]. It differs from standard back-propagation by modulating the gradient flow of the transmission color component using a local variance-based gating factor, ensuring that the forward pass remains visually identical to the original model [13432-specular-aware-gradient-gating]. Choose this when training on scenes with significant specular highlights and semi-transparency. See [Specular-Aware Gradient Gating](13432-specular-aware-gradient-gating.md).

### [Deferred Back-propagation](13506-deferred-back-propagation.md)
A memory-efficient technique for optimizing radiance fields using image losses that require full-resolution inputs, such as VGG-based style losses or Gram-matrix losses [13506-deferred-back-propagation]. Unlike sparse pixel sampling, which is insufficient for CNN-based losses, this method enables full-resolution optimization by decoupling the loss computation from the differentiable rendering pass [13506-deferred-back-propagation]. It sets itself apart by maintaining the memory footprint of a small patch while correctly computing gradients for the entire image, avoiding the geometric inaccuracies and lack of style details associated with sparse sampling [13506-deferred-back-propagation]. Choose this when using full-resolution perceptual or style losses. See [Deferred Back-propagation](13506-deferred-back-propagation.md).

### Backward Pass in Half Precision
A gradient computation method using half-precision (FP16) arithmetic to optimize accuracy-throughput trade-off, omitting block-local reductions [S1, unofficial]. It calculates $\frac{\partial I}{\partial M_i}$ using Eqs. (3, 4, 5), $\frac{\partial M_i}{\partial u}$ using Eq. (2) and bilinear interpolation, and $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i}, \frac{\partial v}{\partial x_i}, \frac{\partial u}{\partial y_i}, \frac{\partial v}{\partial y_i}, \frac{\partial u}{\partial s_i}, \frac{\partial v}{\partial s_i}, \frac{\partial u}{\partial \theta_i}, \frac{\partial v}{\partial \theta_i}$ from Eq. (1) [S1, unofficial]. The gradient of image $I$ w.r.t. primitive position $x_i$ is $\frac{\partial I(x,y)}{\partial x_i} = \frac{\partial I(x,y)}{\partial M_i(x,y)} \left( \frac{\partial M_i(x,y)}{\partial u} \frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i} + \frac{\partial M_i(x,y)}{\partial v} \frac{\partial v}{\partial x_i} \right)$, where $M_i$ is the primitive mask, $u,v$ are local coordinates, and $x_i$ is position [S1, unofficial]. It differs from standard implementations by using half precision and omitting block-local reductions to align with accuracy-throughput goals [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The method originates from the foundational work on differentiable volume rendering and splatting, specifically adapted for 3D Gaussian Splatting. The specific implementation details regarding `half2` atomicAdd, tile-based CUDA pipelines, and the omission of block-local reductions are described in "DiffBMP: Differentiable Rendering with Bitmap Primitives" [S1, unofficial]. This approach enables efficient GPU-accelerated training by leveraging the parallelism of modern graphics hardware for gradient accumulation.
